item.title: The Bitcoin Passport Index: Buying Citizenship in the 21st Century
item.description:

item.title: A Day in the Life of Alex in AnCapville
item.description:
What would a day look like with no state, no taxes, no police monopoly, and no central bank? Through the eyes of an ordinary man named Alex, we tour a society built entirely on voluntary contracts, private property, reputation markets, and competing arbitration firms. Roads are privately owned with risk-based insurance pricing. Schools are parent-funded co-ops competing on outcomes. Money is gold-backed digital currency with no inflation tax. When Alex's cousin commits a violent crime, the system treats it as a tort against the victim with restitution enforced through private labour centres competing on humane conditions. The framework draws on Murray Rothbard's natural order, Stephan Kinsella's property rights and tort-based common law, Hans-Hermann Hoppe's covenant communities, and Bob Murphy's Austrian economics. The episode is honest about the trade-offs: reputation scores can be manipulated, exclusionary communities can become insular, and people who refuse all contracts find themselves frozen out of society. The real question AnCapville forces you to answer is whether you trust yourself more than you trust the people who currently hold the monopoly.

item.title: Closing Claude Code's Feedback Loop — Self-Checking Before Handoff
item.description:
The average developer spends nearly half their coding session babysitting an AI assistant, asking it to try again, fix the same bug, or correct a syntax error it should have caught itself. The traditional workflow is a turn-based loop that feels productive but is actually manual quality control the model could handle on its own. Modern AI models can watch type checkers fail, read test suite output, parse runtime errors, and recognise when something does not compile. The problem is that most verification signals exist outside the codebase. Custom skills encode those verification steps directly into the workflow so the model catches failures before you ever see them. Multi-agent review adds a second layer of objectivity. Composite workflows compose specialised skills into a shipping pipeline that requires minimal human intervention. The principle is simple: hand off as much verification as possible, step in only when genuine judgment is required.

item.title: Istanbul Real Estate: Renovation Costs and ROI for Turkish CBI
item.description:
A practical guide to Istanbul real estate investment for Turkish citizenship by investment. We generalise the renovation cost framework — from cosmetic refreshes at 30 to 50 thousand dollars to full structural overhauls at 140 thousand plus — and explain how to calculate net rental yield after management fees, vacancy, and maintenance. Long-term USD-denominated leases deliver around 5.5 percent net yield; short-term Airbnb lets push toward 7 percent but with higher management overhead. New builds versus renovated resale properties each carry different risk profiles: new builds are move-in ready with no renovation period, while renovated properties in gentrifying neighbourhoods near prime districts offer better price per square metre and stronger appreciation potential. The neighbourhood strategy matters — invest adjacent to established luxury zones where gentrification is spreading. The three-year holding requirement for CBI means your exit strategy must be planned at entry.

Zero Trust for AI Agents — Anthropic Security Framework
item.description:
Anthropic published a 35-page security framework in May 2026 that applies Zero Trust principles to autonomous AI agents in the enterprise. The premise is blunt: perimeter-based security is dead, AI models have compressed exploit timelines from months to hours, and agents make every existing access control model look like a suggestion. The framework introduces least agency — a term from OWASP extending least privilege to restrict what each agent tool can do, how often, and where. It maps controls across three tiers (Foundation, Enterprise, Advanced) covering agent identity, access control, resource isolation, observability, behavioral monitoring, input validation, integrity, and recovery. The Foundation floor has been raised: static API keys are treated as already compromised, short-lived tokens and cryptographic identity are entry requirements. The threat landscape covers prompt injection, tool poisoning via MCP servers, tool chaining attacks, memory poisoning, and supply chain risks including malicious models. Implementation follows eight phases from requirements through supply chain management to defensive operations. Anthropic closes with Agentic SOAR — AI agents handling evidence collection and documentation while humans stay on containment decisions. The uncomfortable question the framework raises but does not answer: who sets the trust boundaries when agents decide how to interpret your instructions?

item.title: OpenHands — Open Source AI Software Engineer
item.description:
OpenHands, originally called OpenDevin, launched from Carnegie Mellon research and has accumulated 75,000 GitHub stars, raised 18.8 million dollars, and become the open-source answer to autonomous coding agents. Unlike autocomplete tools, OpenHands runs agents that plan, act, observe, and reflect in a loop inside sandboxed Docker containers with real code editors, shells, browsers, and task planners. The Software Agent SDK is a composable Python framework that separates model intelligence from agent capability, letting you swap Claude for GPT for Llama without rewriting agent logic. Use cases include vulnerability remediation, COBOL-to-Java migration, incident triage, and PR review. The OpenHands Index, launched January 2026, is the first broad-coverage benchmark for agentic software engineering, revealing that context management is the key differentiator, not raw model size. Enterprise deployment runs on-premise or air-gapped with full audit trails. An AMD partnership brings local inference on Ryzen AI hardware. The honest limit: OpenHands excels at well-scoped, verifiable tasks and struggles with ambiguous requirements and deep domain knowledge. The community recommendation is autonomous agents for 80 percent of backend work, interactive IDE tools for debugging and refinement.

item.title: Liberland 2026 Master Plan
item.description:
Vít Jedlička delivered his 2026 New Year address with a concrete forty million dollar investment plan for the Baranja region surrounding Liberland. The speech covered three strategic pillars. First, legitimacy through citizens in power: Javier Milei governing Argentina, Peter Mitsinka as Czech Foreign Minister, and Somaliland gaining recognition after being first to recognize Liberland in 2017. Second, blockchain governance infrastructure: Justin Sun re-elected as Prime Minister, bringing Tron ecosystem resources, with 2026 priorities on blockchain bridges to centralized financial systems and DAO-based company registration. Third, financial services: Liberland Bank and Liberland Pay launching as centralized banking complements to the decentralized governance layer. The citizenship target is one million applicants. The budget is projected to double. The dual architecture — decentralized governance with centralized financial plumbing — mirrors the same pattern successful crypto exchanges use, applied to a nation-state with territorial sovereignty as its regulatory advantage. Whether Serbia and Croatia accept the economic partnership offer for Baranja is the open question.

item.title: AI Made Us Faster. That Was the Problem
item.description:
David Fowler, a distinguished engineer at Microsoft leading the .NET Aspire team, published the most honest account yet of what AI-first engineering looks like inside a production team. His team produced what felt like six months of code in one week — and he calls it an overconfidence problem. Production got cheaper but maintenance did not. The bottleneck moved from production capacity to judgment capacity. Experienced engineers feel regression when adopting AI agents, not because the tools are bad but because rebuilding your workflow around a new toolchain feels like putting training wheels back on. Fowler introduces the concept of agent-readiness as codebase health: agents work best with clear structure, good tests, and enough context to verify their own work. Without breakthroughs in memory and continuity, human operators still carry the accumulated product context, architectural intent, and team tradeoffs. AI accelerates the work. Engineers still own the result.

item.title: Claude Code Session Management: A Clean Context Beats a Long Context
item.description:
Thariq Shihipar from Anthropic's Claude Code team published the definitive guide to session management with a 1 million token context window — and the core insight is counterintuitive: having more context does not mean you should use it. Context rot starts degrading model performance well before you hit the limit, with accuracy dropping at just 25 percent of the window. The playbook gives you five moves after every turn: continue, rewind with Esc Esc to drop failed attempts, compact with a hint to shed weight mid-task, clear for a fresh session, and subagents for isolated work that only returns conclusions. The rewind habit is described as the number one pro move: instead of correcting a failed approach, jump back to before it happened and redirect with what you learned. Compact proactively at 50 percent, not reactively at 90, because the model is at its least intelligent when autocompact fires under a bloated context. Subagents are the most underrated tool: they get their own clean context window, do all the messy exploration, and only send back the final result. A clean context beats a long context every time.

item.title: Build a System That Prompts Itself
item.description:
An Anthropic engineer said the quiet part out loud: you are not supposed to prompt Claude, you are supposed to build a system that prompts itself. The quote went viral because it named something most people were already doing wrong. The shift is from manual prompting to CLAUDE.md configuration files to fully autonomous agent loops where the system reads your git history, loads your project context, and runs until the task is done without you typing a word. Anthropic calls this context engineering — the discipline of designing the entire information environment an agent operates in. The March 2026 source code leak revealed KAIROS, an unreleased always-on daemon mode referenced 150 times in the codebase. When autonomous agents start writing their own prompts, discarding context they deem unimportant, and making decisions while you sleep, the question is not whether this is powerful. The question is who audits the prompts.

item.title: Boris Cyrulnik on Civilization, Resilience, and Child Development
item.description:
Boris Cyrulnik, the French neuropsychiatrist who coined the term resilience, delivers a sweeping analysis of modern civilization and its unintended consequences. He draws a key distinction between culture (stable institutions like law, architecture, and marriage) and civilization (the shifting conventions of language, rituals, and social norms). The first 1,000 days of a child's life fundamentally structure temperament — modern neuroimaging shows that sensory and verbal deprivation in infants causes measurable prefrontal lobe atrophy, particularly in boys, crippling their ability to regulate impulses. Every civilizational advance carries secondary effects: screens multiply depression risk fourfold, scheduled C-sections deny babies beneficial microbiome exposure, and women's liberation paradoxically dissolves the family structures that once provided stability. Cyrulnik warns of an empathy crisis driven by personal-development culture's egocentrism and proposes art, literature, and Finnish-style education reform as antidotes. A profound meditation on what we gain and what we lose with every step forward.

item.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of HTML for AI Agents
item.description:
Thariq Shihipar, the engineering lead for Claude Code at Anthropic, published a blog post that hit 4.4 million views in 16 hours arguing that HTML outperforms Markdown for AI agent outputs. item.title: Karpathy's LLM Wiki: Build Your Own Knowledge Base
item.description:
Andrej Karpathy published a single GitHub Gist called llm-wiki.md that reframes personal knowledge management using the oldest trick in software engineering: compilation. Your raw sources are source code, the wiki is the compiled binary, and the AI is the compiler. The three-layer architecture keeps raw sources immutable at the bottom, an AI-owned wiki of entity pages, concept pages, and cross-links in the middle, and a schema file like CLAUDE.md at the top that turns a generic agent into a disciplined wiki maintainer. Three operations power the whole thing: ingest drops a source and the AI updates 10 to 15 pages at once, query reads the pre-synthesised wiki instead of raw documents, and lint audits for contradictions, orphans, and stale data. Knowledge compounds over time rather than starting from scratch on every query. The pattern echoes Garry Tan's GBrain system indexing 146,000 pages and the Hermes agent's own llm-wiki skill with Obsidian. The deeper lineage goes back to Vannevar Bush's 1945 Memex vision — a personal knowledge store where connections between documents matter as much as the documents themselves. The bookkeeping that killed every previous wiki is exactly what AI automates. Your knowledge stays on your machine, in markdown, with no cloud dependency and no vendor lock-in.
